client: I’ve been feeling really overwhelmed lately because I’m so stressed about keeping my scholarship this term. After getting that disappointing grade on my final project last semester, I feel like I can’t afford to mess up again, but the pressure is making it hard to focus. I’m not sure if talking about this will actually help me perform better—it feels like something I just have to figure out on my own.
therapist: "I hear how much pressure you're putting on yourself about maintaining your scholarship, and how that disappointing grade from last semester is still weighing on you. While your words express determination, I notice your voice sounds a bit deflated—like part of you might be feeling worn down by all this pressure. Have you noticed moments where the stress feels more manageable versus when it feels overwhelming?"
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, I guess the stress feels more manageable when I’m actually getting work done and things are going well. But lately, it’s been overwhelming almost all the time, especially when I sit down to study and my mind starts racing about what could go wrong. I don’t know how to stop thinking about failing—it’s like I can’t trust myself to do well anymore.
therapist: "It sounds like the fear of failing is taking up a lot of mental space, especially when you’re trying to focus. Even though you know you’re capable when things are going well, that self-doubt seems to creep in and make it harder to trust yourself. What’s one small step you could take to feel more in control when those racing thoughts start?"
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I could try making a study schedule, I guess, but part of me feels like that won’t help because the problem isn’t really about time management—it’s this constant fear that even if I do everything right, I’ll still fail. Sometimes I think "what’s the point" before I even start working.
therapist: "It sounds like you’re stuck in a cycle where the fear of failure overshadows your ability to take action, even when you have practical ideas like a study schedule. That ‘what’s the point’ feeling can be really paralyzing. What do you think might shift if you focused less on the outcome and more on taking one small step at a time?"
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I see what you're saying, but it's hard not to focus on the outcome when my whole future feels like it's riding on this scholarship. When I try to take small steps, part of me just keeps screaming "but what if it's not enough?" Maybe if I could quiet that voice down first... though I don't know how.
therapist: "It sounds like that ‘what if it’s not enough’ voice is really loud and persistent, making it hard to focus on anything else. When you say ‘quiet that voice down,’ what might that look like for you—even just for a moment?"
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I don’t know, maybe if I could remind myself that I’ve done well before and I’m capable, but it feels like those thoughts don’t stick. The fear just takes over again. It’s like my brain doesn’t believe the positive stuff, even if I try to tell myself it’s true.
therapist: "It sounds like you’re trying to counter those fearful thoughts with reminders of your past successes, but the fear keeps pulling you back. When you say your brain doesn’t believe the positive stuff, what do you think might help those reminders feel more convincing?"
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I don’t know what would make those reminders feel more convincing—I feel like I’ve tried everything. Even when I tell myself I’ve succeeded before, part of me thinks, "Yeah, but that was then, what if I can’t do it now?" It’s like my brain always finds a way to twist things back to doubt.
therapist: "It seems like no matter how much you remind yourself of past successes, that doubt keeps finding a way to creep back in. What do you think it would take for you to feel even a little bit more confident in your ability to handle this, despite those doubts?"
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Maybe if I could see some small wins along the way, like getting positive feedback on an assignment or feeling like I’m making progress, it would help. But even then, I worry that I’ll just dismiss those wins as luck or something. It’s like I don’t trust myself to be consistent, even when things go well.
therapist: "It sounds like you’re caught in a pattern where even small wins don’t feel fully convincing, and that self-doubt keeps creeping back in. What do you think it would take to start trusting those wins as evidence of your ability, rather than dismissing them as luck?"
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I don’t know, honestly. Even when I do get positive feedback, it’s like my brain immediately downplays it or finds reasons why it doesn’t count. I think part of me feels like I need to be perfect to prove I’m good enough, and anything less feels like failure. It’s exhausting, but I don’t know how to break out of that mindset.
therapist: "It sounds like you’re holding yourself to such a high standard that even positive feedback doesn’t feel like enough—like anything short of perfect still feels like failure. That constant striving for perfection must be exhausting. What do you think might shift if you allowed yourself to see ‘good enough’ as truly good enough?"
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I don’t know if I can even imagine what "good enough" would feel like—it’s like my brain doesn’t have a setting for that. Even if I tried to accept it, I’d probably just feel guilty or like I’m settling for less. I think part of me believes that if I don’t aim for perfection, I’ll lose everything I’ve worked for.
therapist: "It sounds like the idea of ‘good enough’ feels almost impossible to imagine, and that aiming for anything less than perfection brings up a lot of fear and guilt. What do you think it would take to start seeing ‘good enough’ not as settling, but as a way to take care of yourself while still working toward your goals?"
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess I’d need to stop seeing "good enough" as a failure, but that’s easier said than done. It’s like my whole mindset is wired to think that anything less than perfect means I’m not trying hard enough. Even the idea of taking care of myself feels selfish—like I should be pushing harder, not easing up. It’s hard to imagine how to change that.
therapist: "It sounds like shifting your mindset feels really challenging, especially when ‘good enough’ feels so tied to failure and self-doubt. That idea of taking care of yourself feeling selfish—could that be part of what’s keeping you stuck in this cycle of pushing harder and harder?"
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech
